data.title: AstraZeneca Gets FDA Approval for Bladder Cancer Treatment
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

AstraZeneca received Food and Drug Administration approval for its drug Imfinzi in combination with other therapies as a treatment for patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

The approval is for Imfinzi used in combination with enfortumab vedotin-ejfv as neoadjuvant treatment, followed by Imfinzi monotherapy as adjuvant treatment after bladder-removal cancer.

The approval is based on results from the Volga Phase 3 trial. Treated patients in the trial demonstrated a 49% reduction in the risk of disease progression or recurrence.

Results from the key secondary endpoint of overall survival showed that the Imfinzi combination reduced the risk of death by 42% compared to the comparison arm.

Write to Katherine Hamilton at katherine.hamilton@wsj.com

data.title: More Than 10,000 Flights Delayed or Canceled in FAA's Nationwide Groundstop— WSJ
data.description:
By Andrew Tangel, Jacob Passy and Alison Sider

The Federal Aviation Administration halted departing flights nationwide Friday afternoon, citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns after air-traffic control communications were disrupted.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote on X that there had been a communication issue affecting multiple air route traffic-control centers, which handle high-altitude flights covering large swaths of the country. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue," he wrote.

Planes in the air are able to continue flying to their destinations, an FAA spokeswoman said. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case-by-case basis, the agency said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House on Friday that "there was no prior indication, or indication as of yet, that this was a nefarious attack against us. This is a telecommunications outage as of now." When asked if it could be a cyberattack, Mullin said officials weren't ruling anything out yet.

"There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," Mullin said, adding this isn't "another 9/11."

The groundstop started Friday afternoon at 3:53 p.m. ET. More than 1,100 U.S. flights had been canceled and nearly 10,000 had been delayed as of Friday at 5:40 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware. As of around 4 p.m., there were still roughly 11,000 flights scheduled to depart from U.S. airports Friday, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.

Disruptions are likely to grow. With departures halted, airports fill up, leaving little room for more flights to land. Nearly 500 flights returned to the airport they took off from as of 5:50 pm ET Friday, and more than 100 diverted to another airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics firm.

That leaves planes and crew members out of place for their next flights, which could create cascading scheduling problems into the weekend.

Some international departures from the east and west coasts were being allowed to take off Friday evening, according to industry officials.

At Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, word quickly spread among travelers while ground traffic appeared to suddenly stop on the tarmac late Friday afternoon. By early evening, telecom issues at some FAA air-traffic facilities were coming back online, according to people familiar with the matter.

The outage appears to be affecting a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to people briefed on the matter. The network handles crucial radio frequencies that air-traffic controllers use to communicate with pilots, the people said. It wasn't immediately clear whether the outage also affected the radar feeds that controllers use to keep aircraft safely separated in the skies.

An L3Harris spokeswoman didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

United Airlines said it is responding to the groundstop and will work with customers to get them to destinations once the issue is resolved. American said it expects its schedule to be disrupted for the rest of the day, depending how long the groundstop remains in place.

"It will be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible when the FAA lifts this ground stop," American said in a statement.

Several airlines issued waivers to allow travelers to rebook flights without penalty. At some airports, including New York's LaGuardia, travelers whose flights were cancelled had to wait in long lines to get their checked bags back before they could go home. At Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, security lines were empty as people milled about checking their phones for updates.

John Sturino, a musician who plays the drums, said he is going to miss a percussion convention in Indianapolis because of the flight delay. The Brooklyn native said he had been waiting half an hour in line to cancel his flight at the Delta lounge desk in LaGuardia Airport and get a refund.

"It wasn't worth staying in the airport," he said.

Sara Garven, 66, was traveling with her husband home to Wisconsin from Sarasota, Fla., when the couple were stranded in Baltimore where they had a layover. Overhead announcements were being made roughly every 30 minutes, she said, but the information was no different from what was available online.

"Some are sprinkling the Friday the 13th component, which isn't really helping," she said. "Our main concern is just getting home safely."

This is the second time in recent years the FAA has taken the extraordinary step of halting all departures across the country.

In 2023, a nationwide groundstop was ordered amid an outage of the FAA's Notice to Airmen system, which provides critical information to pilots. That order lasted for two hours, contributing to more than 1,000 flight cancellations. Before that, the FAA had only taken that step on Sept. 11, 2001.

The nation's air-traffic control system has been beset by communications issues leading to radio and radar outages that have affected various FAA facilities in recent years. Earlier this year, flights at New York-area airports were halted when a contractor accidentally cut a fiber communications line in New Jersey.

Other outages that have affected the Dallas area, Upper Midwest and New York City area have been relatively contained.

data.title: The Chaos and Unexpected Joys of a 19-Hour Global Email Outage — WSJ
data.description:
By Robert McMillan and Angel Au-Yeung

We may live in an age of messaging apps and artificial intelligence, but as about half a billion people discovered this week, good old-fashioned email is pretty important, too.

Starting around 12:30 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, a Microsoft cloud outage knocked the company's email and other services offline. The interruption left swaths of the globe, from healthcare systems to stock exchanges to members of U.K. Parliament, without one of their main tools for communicating. It was the tech world's equivalent of a snow day.

The cause was a server upgrade gone wrong, which then cascaded globally. It was a day reminiscent of the chaos caused in 2024 when the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike crashed 8.5 million Windows systems.

Some users were frustrated. Some simply checked out from work. Others time-traveled back to the telephone era.

Support staff at Envision Technology Advisors, a technical services company, spent yesterday on the phone explaining to customers why their email wasn't working, said Stephen Rose, the company's chief technology officer.

Invision's customers began reaching out early in the day, but with email cut off, they had to turn to the telephone, Rose said. So they called. "Our service desk got totally paralyzed," he said.

Rose's team told callers that Envision wasn't to blame for the outage; Microsoft was. "You hope that it gets out by word of telephone," he said.

Email-deprived entities around the world encouraged customers to reach out via phone, including a water utility in Halifax, Nova Scotia; Detroit's light-rail system; and the East Gippsland region of Australia.

In the U.S., city governments across the country lost email, including Tampa, Fla.; Louisville, Ky.; and the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner. The House of Representatives was hit too. As was the shipping company Maersk and European exchange operator Euronext. In England, the National Health Service was among several government agencies affected by the outage.

The Lincolnshire Partnership NHS Foundation Trust, a British publicly funded healthcare provider that specializes in mental health services, put out a press release with instructions for patients during the outage. "We would ask that if you need to make a referral today, or you are experiencing a crisis please call our services rather than email at this time," the statement said.

The outage affected a range of Microsoft 365 services, but it centered on Exchange Online and email services, Microsoft said.

Microsoft Teams, a messaging and video chat platform, remained up for many, prompting complaints. "Dear @ Microsoft - you shut down the wrong one. Please turn our email back on and kill Teams. Sincerely, Everyone," wrote Steve Schale, a political strategist based in Florida, on X.

For Jeffrey Michelson, a partner at an accounting firm based in New York City, the outage became a welcome chance to check a few items off his to-do list.

Michelson noticed he wasn't getting any new emails in his inbox in the early afternoon on Thursday. After dropping his daughter off at karate lessons just before sunset, he realized he might not be receiving emails for the rest of the evening.

So he got to work building two bookshelves that his wife had been asking him to complete for a month. "It was kind of nice, I'm not gonna lie," said Michelson. The next day, he woke up in the early morning to 70 unread emails.

Like any snow day, Thursday was fun for some but not so great for people who depended on Microsoft's cloud to get their work done. "Kids love a snow day," Envision's Rose said. "Parents go, 'Oh, my God, I've got these kids inside the house all day.' It's all a matter of perspective."

The outage was more disruptive for some than others. Workhorse Group, an industrial company based in the Detroit area, had to reschedule its third-quarter earnings call to the following week because of the outage.

"Our experience (clearly, like many others) shows how vital it is to have real-time communications, access to documents and the ability to share documents with others," said company spokesman John Williams. He sent his comment via text message.

A Microsoft spokesman said the company wasn't hacked. It was a network upgrade gone wrong, he said. "Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration," he said.

The blackout lasted about 19 hours, said Doug Madory, head of internet analysis at the networking company Infoblox.

On X, Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella was silent on the outage. That is not a complete surprise. "I'm an email typist," he told Bloomberg last year.

Write to Robert McMillan at robert.mcmillan@wsj.com and Angel Au-Yeung at angel.au-yeung@wsj.com

data.title: SpaceX launches 15th Starship flight with hopes of achieving first round trip
data.description:
Key points:
  • SpaceX plans attempt at first return-landing catch of Starship on Saturday
  • Test is key to Musk's effort to produce fully reusable rocket ship
  • Starship delivering its second batch of satellites to orbit

By Joey Roulette

SpaceX launched the 15th flight of its Starship spacecraft from Texas on Friday on a mission the company hopes will be the first round-trip rocket voyage to orbit and back to the very spot where it left Earth, a key test of Elon Musk's effort to build a fully reusable rocket system.

Plans call for Starship's uncrewed upper-stage vessel to re-enter the atmosphere after nearly a day in orbit and return to its launch tower on Saturday for an engine-controlled touchdown assisted by the giant mechanical arms of a pioneering catch-landing mechanism.

SpaceX had intended to use the same return-flight and "chopstick"-arm technology to recover Starship's lower-stage booster rocket shortly after the two parts of the spacecraft separated within minutes of the launch.

But the Super Heavy booster, for reasons not immediately clear, was diverted from its return flight path to a fixed point over the Gulf of Mexico and momentarily hovered in the air before exploding a short distance over the sea surface.

SpaceX mission controllers hoped to have better luck in steering Starship's upper stage back to home base at the end of its flight. The vehicle reached orbit about 27 minutes after launch, SpaceX said.

KEY TEST OF REUSABILITY

Bringing the top portion of the spacecraft intact back to the platform where it was launched would mark a breakthrough in the ambitions of Musk, who founded SpaceX in 2002, to reduce spaceflight costs by developing a fully recyclable rocket system.

The combined vehicle, consisting of the main Starship cargo-and-crew vessel perched atop its Super Heavy booster rocket and standing 40 stories high, roared off its launch pad from SpaceX's South Texas Starbase complex along the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville.

The flight marked Starship's 15th test flight since 2023 and the second to carry a batch of operational Starlink satellites to orbit. That makes the mission both a revenue-generating endeavor for SpaceX's satellite-connectivity business and a high-stakes test for a rocket ship still under development.

Starship 15 began releasing its cargo of 26 satellites about 36 minutes into its flight in a payload-delivery operation expected to take less than an hour to complete, the company said in a livestream presentation of the mission.

Musk's space and AI business views Starship as key to expanding its network of Starlink internet satellites and, in the future, deploying a swarm of orbital AI data-processing centers dubbed Starmind, as the company positions itself to become a high-tech infrastructure provider.

SpaceX last launched Starship in September, taking the rocket and a payload of satellites to orbit for the first time despite some rocket engines shutting down mid-flight. That mission, planned to last 10 hours, ended after roughly three hours with an upper stage splashing down intact into the Pacific Ocean before bursting into flames.

RETURN-FLIGHT AND RECOVERY PLANS

For Friday's mission, the company was aiming for both the lower-stage Super Heavy and the upper-stage Starship to return to the spacecraft's Texas launch site for safe landing and recovery. Plans called for the orbital cruise vessel to touch down about 22 hours after launch. SpaceX has said it would be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" if that feat is achieved.

SpaceX has previously returned the 236-foot (72-meter) Super Heavy booster three times to its launch pad after sending Starship to space, with the booster flying itself back to Earth minutes after launch and gently descending upright into the grasp of a pair of large mechanical arms fixed to the launch tower. The last such "tower catch" was in March 2025.

It was not immediately clear why Friday's attempt failed.

Starship was expected to descend from space after completing 14 orbits around Earth, setting up its debut catch landing for Saturday afternoon.

Musk has said he expects to achieve a pace of weekly Starship launches by the first half of 2027.

NASA has helped fund Starship's development with roughly $3.2 billion since selecting the rocket ship in 2021 to serve as a lunar lander for its astronauts under the multibillion-dollar Artemis moon program. SpaceX has put at least $15 billion of its own funds into the rocket's development.

NASA and SpaceX expect Starship to land humans on the moon by 2028, though several major testing objectives remain that analysts and industry engineers believe will push that timeline back. Those milestones include demonstrating complex fuel transfers between Starship tanker rockets in orbit, a critical process that will enable Starship to travel beyond Earth's orbit to the moon.

Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is also developing a moon lander, Blue Moon, for NASA under the Artemis program. Blue Moon is poised to join Starship and another spacecraft, NASA's Orion capsule, in Earth's orbit next year for Artemis III, a docking test mission before NASA's planned moon landing missions begin with Artemis IV.

data.title: Costco: An AI Shelter? — Barrons.com
data.description:
By George Glover

Fears of a slowdown in artificial-intelligence spending have hit the market like a gale-force storm lately. Looking for shelter? Costco Wholesale shares could shield investors from all that volatility.

The big-box warehouse chain, for instance, is giving stockholders an early holiday present. Late Tuesday, it declared a special cash dividend of $30 — enough to buy you 20 servings of Costco's legendary $1.50 hot dog/soda combo. More good news: Costco also said its board had approved a $4 billion stock buyback program. The market always likes those.

Both developments suggest the stock could be a good defensive play for investors looking for steady returns in these uncertain times. "Strong execution, durable cash generation, and shareholder returns helps explain why investors continue to flock to Costco," Jefferies analyst Corey Tarlowe said in a note.

The results are already in. Hopes of a one-off dividend have helped power the stock 24% higher this year, but even the bulls weren't expecting such a hefty payout. "The special dividend is well above our expectations of about $20 per share," says Oppenheimer's Rupesh Parikh, who has had Costco as a top pick for the past year.

Looking for that rare sort of stock that looks both AI and inflation-proof? You could do a lot worse. And, enjoy the hot dogs.

Write to George Glover at george.glover@dowjones.com

Last Week

Yikes!

Does it get crazier every week, or is it just us? The big news, of course, is the Jensen Huang/Nvidia scandal, driving the stock price of the chip king down 7% moments after the CEO stepped aside on Thursday. But what about collateral damage at the White House? Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was a Huang fan and?is under fire. He survived Epstein Island — he might not survive this.

December Decision

If there was any question about the Fed raising rates at its next meeting in December, it was answered when inflation data came out last week. October's CPI report showed that prices were up 0.4% from the previous month — more than estimates. Influential Fed governor Christopher Waller says it's time for a big hike. As Barron's reporter Naomi Buchanan put it, "Inflation is?hot and investors are bothered."

Fun Fact

Legendary lawyer Stephen Neal isn't just Nvidia's lead independent director, but per The Information, he once represented, at Cooley LLP, Elizabeth Holmes. As it turned out, Cooley/Neal dropped her because they weren't paid. No blood in that rock.

Krafty

New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft won six Super Bowls, but that isn't enough to keep him busy. He's pushing a $16 billion data center in tiny Sutton, Mass. It could be the fourth-largest such complex in?the U.S., says the Boston Globe. Residents are "seething."

Next Week

Tuesday 11/17

Nvidia reports third-quarter fiscal-2027 results, less than a week after the stunning exit of Jensen Huang, Nvidia's co-founder and, until now, its only CEO. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO while also remaining as CFO. Shares of Nvidia are down 32% from their October peak.

S&P 500 index companies also releasing earnings this week include Home Depot and Walt Disney on Tuesday. Lowe's, Palo Alto Networks, Target, and TJX Cos. report their results on Wednesday, while Intuit, Ross Stores, and Walmart do so on Thursday.

The Census Bureau reports retail and food-services sales for October. Consensus estimate is for a 0.2% month-over-month increase, after a 0.8% jump in September. Excluding autos and gas, sales are expected to rise 0.3%, one-tenth of a percentage point more than previously.

Wednesday 11/18

The Federal Open Market Committee releases the minutes from its late-October monetary-policy meeting. At?that meeting, the FOMC left the federal-funds rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4%, with two members dissenting in favor of a quarter of a percentage point rate hike.

The Numbers

30%

Decline in Jensen Huang's net worth, to $138 billion, since hitting an all-time peak on?Oct. 5.

$1 B

Preorders for Grand Theft Auto VI, outpacing every videogame before it; sales begin on Nov. 19.

16

SEC actions against public firms and their units in the 12?months through Sept. 30, the lowest in at least 16 years.

$1.29 T

Americans' credit-card debt, a?record, after climbing by some $22 billion in the third quarter.

data.title: Fed's Jefferson: Further Policy Adjustments Should Be Determined By Carefully Examining Trends in the Data
data.description:
By Jessica Coacci

Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said that further policy adjustments should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

"Data received so far for October remains consistent with well above-target inflation," according to the text of Jefferson's remarks, scheduled to be delivered in San Diego on Friday.

Jefferson said that data received since the Fed's October policy meeting have been consistent with economic activity and labor market conditions remaining broadly solid, while inflation readings show persistent price pressures.

Jefferson also said he remains concerned about the risk of higher energy prices leading to a persistent rise in inflation more broadly.

"Going forward, I believe that further policy adjustments should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks," Jefferson said.

Write to Jessica Coacci at jessica.coacci@wsj.com

As of closing on November 12, 2026 (the "Closing Date"), the Company will be issuing 42,139,400 units (the "Units"), at a price of $0.10 per Unit, each Unit consisting of one common share and one-half share purchase warrant, each whole warrant (the "Warrants") entitling the holder thereof to purchase one additional common share, exercisable for a period of two (2) years from the date of issuance at a price of $0.20 per share.

Proceeds raised will be used toward expenditures required to advance the permitting of the Kinsley Mountain gold property in Nevada, securing the necessary permits to commence preliminary exploration work on the Troy Canyon property, also in Nevada, and general working capital purposes.

In connection with the closing of this Offering, the Company paid cash finders' fees of C$3,780.

All securities issued will be subject to a four-month hold period in accordance with applicable securities laws.

In connection with the Private Placement, certain insiders of the Company (the "Insiders"), acquired 9,000,000 Units, representing 14.76% of the Units sold under the Private Placement. Participation by the Insiders in the Private Placement was considered a "related party transaction" pursuant to Multilateral Instrument 61-101 Protection of Minority Security Holders in Special Transactions ("MI 61-101"). The Company was exempt from the requirements to obtain a formal valuation or minority shareholder approval in connection with the Insiders' participation in the Private Placement pursuant to subsections 5.5(a) and 5.7(1)(a) of MI 61-101, as neither the fair market value of the Units to be issued to, nor the consideration paid by the Insiders exceeded 25% of the Company's market capitalization.

Prior to closing the Offering, the Company was in receipt of a completed subscription agreement, for which funds have not been received. The Company fully expects to receive these funds and will issue an additional press release upon receipt of those funds, at which time the Company will have closed oversubscribed on a total of $5,413,940. The Company will complete the Offering by November 25, 2026.

CopAur is a mine development company backed by an experienced team of resource professionals focused on advancing its flagship Kinsley Mountain Gold Project, a Carlin-style sedimentary gold system located approximately 80 km south of West Wendover, Nevada.

data.title: Coinbase Institutional says Fed rate expectations, not the Binance hack, sank Bitcoin
data.description:
Bitcoin's recent slide has an obvious suspect: the Binance hack. Coinbase Institutional says the evidence points somewhere else.

According to Coinbase Institutional, shifting expectations for Federal Reserve interest rate policy, not the breach at the world's best-known exchange, drove Bitcoin's latest decline.

The pivot point was the Consumer Price Index report released on November 10. Headline consumer prices climbed 0.4% month-over-month, while core CPI, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, rose 0.3%.

Those numbers ran hot enough to reshape bets on what the Fed does next. Market pricing for a 25-basis-point rate increase in December climbed above 90% following the report.

The CME FedWatch tool showed roughly an 88% to 92% probability of that quarter-point hike. Odds of a larger move stayed substantially lower.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller's commentary added to the adjustment, as futures markets digested both the data and the policy signals.

Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 after the CPI release, falling to levels last seen in mid-August. By November 13, it was trading in a range of roughly $67,770 to $68,500.

Leverage made the move uglier. Liquidations of leveraged long positions totaled around $1.3 billion to $1.6 billion during the November 13 decline, with overall liquidation levels reported as surpassing $1.6 billion.

Institutional money was heading for the exits too. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded about $1.44 billion to $1.88 billion in net outflows in early November, adding steady selling pressure on top of the leverage flush.

None of this makes the Binance breach a minor event. The October 29 hack drained approximately $6.3 billion in assets, including 18,270 BTC.

The incident did have brief price implications. But in Coinbase Institutional's reading, its effect faded, and the broader macro backdrop did the heavier lifting in Bitcoin's downturn.

Coinbase Institutional's analysis lines up with a growing view that Bitcoin now trades more on interest rates, inflation, and dollar strength than on isolated incidents within the industry.

The ETF outflows deserve close attention. Spot Bitcoin ETFs saw net outflows in the range of $1.44 billion to $1.88 billion in early November, showing that this investor base also responds to rising rates and a stronger dollar.

The liquidation figures carry their own warning. Heavy leverage amplifies every macro surprise, turning a modest repricing into a sharp drop.

The key variables to monitor are clear enough: the next inflation readings, the Fed's December decision, ETF flow trends, and how much leverage rebuilds in derivatives markets. If Coinbase Institutional is right, those factors will say more about Bitcoin's next move than any single exchange incident.

data.title: AstraZeneca Gets FDA Approval for Bladder Cancer Treatment
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

AstraZeneca received Food and Drug Administration approval for its drug Imfinzi in combination with other therapies as a treatment for patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

The approval is for Imfinzi used in combination with enfortumab vedotin-ejfv as neoadjuvant treatment, followed by Imfinzi monotherapy as adjuvant treatment after bladder-removal cancer.

The approval is based on results from the Volga Phase 3 trial. Treated patients in the trial demonstrated a 49% reduction in the risk of disease progression or recurrence.

Results from the key secondary endpoint of overall survival showed that the Imfinzi combination reduced the risk of death by 42% compared to the comparison arm.

data.title: JPMorgan's Top Credit Cards Executive Is Leaving the Bank — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Rebecca Ungarino

The executive responsible for JPMorgan Chase's vast credit card business, among the largest in the world, is leaving the bank, according to an internal memo viewed by Barron's.

Allison Beer, the CEO of card and connected commerce, "has informed me of her decision to leave the firm for an external opportunity," JPMorgan Co-President Troy Rohrbaugh said in a memo on Friday.

"She and her team have played an important part in moving our card business to where it is today," he said in the memo to employees.

Beer's exit is notable because she is among the most powerful leaders in the credit card industry. JPMorgan's card business is among the world's largest by customer spending and balances. She is leaving for another company at a moment when banks are fiercely competing to win over cardholders, especially those who are higher earners.

Rohrbaugh's team plans to name a new leader for the card and connected commerce businesses in the coming weeks, he wrote. In the meantime, those who reported to Beer will report to Rohrbaugh, who is the CEO of consumer and community banking.

A JPMorgan spokesman declined to specify who will replace Beer. Beer didn't immediately respond to Barron's request for comment.

Beer joined JPMorgan in 2017 as a top payments executive from American Express.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

data.title: Stocks mostly ease with tech, Nvidia concerns; airline shares fall late in session
data.description:
Key points:
  • Nasdaq, S&P 500 end lower
  • Oil prices decline for the week
  • Dollar extends gains

By Caroline Valetkevitch and Elizabeth Howcroft

Stock indexes mostly fell on Friday as technology shares sold off amid concerns about US chipmaker Nvidia , while the dollar was at a 19-month high.

Airline shares dropped in the final minutes of the regular US session after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop of all departing flights. The agency said this was "due to extraordinary circumstance and reasons for safety" after it earlier reported serious air traffic control communications issues. The NYSE Arca airline index closed down 1.4%.

The Nasdaq and S&P 500 ended lower, but all three of the major US stock indexes and the pan-European STOXX 600 registered gains for the week.

Jensen Huang's resignation on Thursday as Nvidia CEO could have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy and the broader AI industry and supply chain given his push to preserve access to the Chinese market and close ties with US President Donald Trump. Huang stepped down after revelations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for China.

The Financial Times reported that Nvidia's board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Huang.

The Philadelphia semiconductor index was down 3.4% and shares of Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were sharply lower. Nvidia shares finished 2% lower.

"Traders probably weren't excited about carrying positions into the weekend," said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana.

"A lot of attention is still going to be paid next week to Nvidia," he said. The company is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday after the closing bell.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 50.46 points, or 0.10%, to 52,347.55, the S&P 500 CBOE:SPX fell 30.73 points, or 0.40%, to 7,561.67 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 229.82 points, or 0.91%, to 25,136.27. The Nasdaq and S&P 500 both snapped a four-week streak of declines.

MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe EURONEXT:IACWI fell 4.15 points, or 0.37%, to 1,112.12.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index ended up just 0.02%, but recorded its best week since late June as strong earnings and a rotation out of tech globally helped investors look past geopolitical risks and the volatility involving AI stocks.

A global outage of Microsoft Outlook and Teams was easing on Friday after more than 24 hours of disruption crippled online communications across businesses and governments, though the company said it still had no timeline for full recovery of services.

US 2-YEAR YIELDS HAVE LARGEST WEEKLY RISE IN OVER TWO YEARS

The US dollar index gained for a fourth straight day. Traders this week have been ramping up bets on faster interest rate increases following the consumer price data and hawkish Federal Reserve official commentary.

The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.17% to 103.40. It hit its highest since April 2025. The euro was down 0.29% at $1.1021.

Investors digested a report showing the US October Producer Price Index for final demand was slightly softer than expected, but still shot up 6.5% year over year. It followed a hotter-than-expected US consumer prices reading earlier this week.

Traders see rising odds that the US central bank could hike rates by a larger-than-usual 50 basis points in December, or raise rates by 25 basis points at each of the next three meetings.

"Inflation is stubbornly high and the Fed's going to need to act a little bit quicker and a little bit more aggressively," said Molly Brooks, US rates strategist at TD Securities.

Fed funds futures traders are pricing in an 11% chance of a 50-basis-point hike at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting, which was seen as having zero probability a week ago, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch Tool.

Treasury yields briefly dipped after the PPI data, but interest-rate-sensitive 2-year Treasury yields had the largest weekly increase in over two years.

The 2-year note (US2YT=RR) yield was last up 0.34 basis point at 4.867%. It earlier reached 4.892%, the highest since October 14. It registered the biggest weekly increase since the first week of October 2024.

Oil prices were little changed on Friday, but declined for a second straight week. Washington's focus on blockading Iran and ramping up other economic pressures allayed fears of renewed direct conflict in the Iran war.

Brent futures settled at $95.84 a barrel, up 2 cents, or 0.02%. US West Texas Intermediate futures finished at $88.56 a barrel, down 18 cents, or 0.20%. Both Brent and US crude declined for the week.

data.title: SpaceX Launches Starship on Ambitious Bid to Catch Spacecraft — WSJ
data.description:
By Drew FitzGerald

SpaceX's Starship headed to orbit Friday on a mission to prove it can ferry massive payloads into space before softly landing back on Earth.

The more than 400-foot-tall experimental rocket launched from SpaceX's Texas space port around 4:50 p.m. local time Friday on its 15th mission.

But the mission failed its first big test — having the new booster return to the launchpad. SpaceX identified an issue after the booster separated from the spacecraft, and the booster was diverted to crash into the waters near the launchpad.

The spaceship, which continued its trip, is slated to deliver another batch of Starlink satellites into low-Earth-orbit before returning to the same pad Saturday afternoon.

Capturing Starship's booster and cargo vessel on the same mission would have been a first for the rocket company. SpaceX has previously caught an earlier version of its Super Heavy booster but hadn't attempted to land its latest design. The company has never recovered the Starship cargo vessel on land for later reuse.

SpaceX Chief Executive Elon Musk last month said that pulling off both maneuvers would be a "profound technology milestone."

SpaceX already pioneered low-cost spaceflight with its smaller Falcon 9 rockets, which have lifted thousands of Starlink internet satellites into orbit. The rocket fleet's reliability has made satellite deployment affordable enough to turn Starlink into a major profit center for the company. But SpaceX has signaled that it plans to wind down the Falcon 9 program to focus on Starship.

Starship has soaked up billions of dollars to develop and test. And so far, it has had a mixed record of success. Its ability to carry 100 metric tons of cargo would make satellite deployment much cheaper — if its engineers can reliably launch and recover the vehicle.

Friday's mission initially called for Starship's new booster to return to its tower, where chopstick-like arms would deploy to catch it as it hovered above the ground. An earlier version of the booster successfully completed that maneuver for the first time in 2024.

The huge spacecraft's heat shield will need to survive extreme re-entry temperatures in order for SpaceX to attempt to recover the vehicle.

Write to Drew FitzGerald at andrew.fitzgerald@wsj.com
